subtype: Small treat seems big or small by comparison [Actor]
passage: At the day-care snack table, Sheela Ma'am handed out plain round biscuits. Gurleen, five, nibbled hers slowly. Then Sheela Ma'am opened a new tin. "Surprise! Chocolate cream ones today." Gurleen got one and squealed, bouncing on her chair. "Best day!" Next, her little brother Nilesh got his, a big round one with a jam heart in the middle. Gurleen's face crumpled. She looked at her small cream biscuit, then at his. Her eyes filled. "His is bigger," she whispered, pushing hers away. A minute ago it had been the best biscuit in the world.

qa.q: What was in the middle of Nilesh's biscuit?
qa.a: A jam heart.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen squeal "Best day!" at first?
qa.a: After the plain biscuit, the chocolate cream one seemed wonderful by comparison, so she felt thrilled.

qa.q: How could Sheela Ma'am help when Gurleen pushes her biscuit away?
qa.a: She could kneel beside her, name the feeling ("You wanted a big one too") and remind her how happy the cream biscuit made her a minute ago.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nilesh when his sister starts crying about his biscuit?
qa.a: Nilesh may feel confused, or a little guilty, holding a big biscuit that has suddenly made his sister sad.

grounding: A young girl is delighted with a cream biscuit after a plain one but tearful when her brother gets a bigger one; the comparison changes the feeling.

subtype: Small treat seems big or small by comparison [Actor]
passage: I'm Irfan, Pooja's big brother. On Sunday, Mummy gave Pooja a small plain rusk, and she ate it without a word. Then Mummy gave her a biscuit with pink icing, and Pooja danced around the kitchen, holding it up like a trophy. Then Mummy gave me a big coconut cookie from the bakery. Pooja stopped dancing. She looked at her pink biscuit, then at my cookie, and her lip wobbled. "It's tiny," she said, and started to cry. Two minutes before, it was the best thing ever. I don't know what changed in her head. The biscuit didn't change at all.

qa.q: What was on the biscuit Mummy gave Pooja?
qa.a: Pink icing.

qa.q: Why did Pooja's lip start to wobble when she saw Irfan's cookie?
qa.a: Next to his big coconut cookie, her pink biscuit suddenly seemed tiny, so she felt sad and left out. 🥺

qa.q: What could Mummy do next time to avoid the tears?
qa.a: She could hand out the treats at the same time, or give similar sizes, and talk with Pooja about how happy the pink biscuit made her.

qa.q: How does Irfan see what happened to his sister?
qa.a: Irfan notices that the biscuit stayed exactly the same and only her feeling changed, though Irfan can't tell what went on inside her head.

grounding: An older brother watches his little sister go from joy to tears over the same biscuit once she compares it with his bigger cookie.

qa.a: On Wednesday, next to Naveen's huge chocolate cookie, it looked like "a baby one" and he was upset; on Friday nothing bigger sat beside it, so he was happy with it as a treat again.

qa.a: She could comfort him, say it's hard when someone else's treat looks bigger, and remind him how much he enjoyed that same jam biscuit the day before.

qa.q: What might Naveen feel when his little brother bursts into tears over the cookie?
qa.a: Naveen might feel awkward or a bit guilty after coming happily from a party, or be tempted to share just to stop the crying.

grounding: Over a few days, a small boy loves a jam biscuit on its own but cries over it when his brother has a bigger cookie.

passage: At the bakery near their Chennai flat, the baker gave Leela, five, a small star-shaped biscuit for free. Leela gasped and held it up to the light. 'A star! Seema Akka, look!' She did a little dance by the glass case. Then the baker handed her big sister Seema a large heart biscuit with pink icing. Leela stopped dancing. She looked at the heart, then at her star. 'Mine is small,' she whispered, eyes filling. Seema knelt. 'Your star was the best thing ever a minute ago.' Leela sniffed and looked at it again.

qa.q: What shape was Leela's free biscuit?
qa.a: It was a small star-shaped biscuit.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she first got the star biscuit?
qa.a: She was delighted, gasping, holding it up to the light and doing a little dance by the glass case.

qa.a: Seema knelt and reminded Leela that her star was the best thing a minute ago, helping her see the same biscuit without comparing it to the heart.

qa.a: The baker might feel sorry, since both biscuits were meant as a kind treat and one ended up making Leela sad.
